reference.source: Stiehm's Immune Deficiencies / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Presents in childhood with chronic non-malignant lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly plus autoimmune cytopenias (haemolytic anaemia, immune thrombocytopenia, neutropenia)
The hallmark laboratory finding is an expanded population of double-negative T cells (CD3-positive, TCR alpha-beta-positive, CD4-negative and CD8-negative)
Caused by defective FAS-mediated apoptosis, so autoreactive lymphocytes that should be deleted persist and accumulate
Germline FAS (TNFRSF6) mutation is the commonest genetic cause; FAS ligand and caspase-10 defects also occur, and somatic FAS mutations are recognised
Supportive biomarkers include raised vitamin B12, soluble FAS ligand, interleukin-10 and interleukin-18
There is a substantially increased lifetime risk of Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma
Immunosuppression targeting the autoimmune cytopenias is used rather than routine splenectomy, which carries added sepsis risk in these patients
reference.pathophysiology: Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome results from impaired programmed cell death (apoptosis) of lymphocytes through the FAS receptor pathway. Under normal circumstances, activated lymphocytes that are no longer needed, including autoreactive clones, are removed when FAS engages its ligand and triggers a caspase-dependent death signal. Mutations affecting FAS, its ligand, or downstream caspase-10 disrupt this deletion, so lymphocytes accumulate, producing chronic lymphoproliferation and a characteristic expansion of immature double-negative T cells. The persistence of autoreactive cells drives autoimmunity, predominantly directed at blood cells, and the failure of a key tumour-suppressive apoptotic checkpoint underlies the elevated lymphoma risk.
additionalDifferentials: Common variable immunodeficiency with autoimmune features
ALPS-like disorders such as RALD, CTLA4 or LRBA deficiency and activated PI3K-delta syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Flow cytometry quantifying double-negative (alpha-beta) T cells
Serum biomarkers including vitamin B12, soluble FAS ligand, interleukin-10 and interleukin-18
Molecular genetic testing of FAS, FASLG and CASP10 including somatic mutation analysis
Full blood count, reticulocytes and direct antiglobulin test for autoimmune cytopenias
Immunoglobulins and lymph node biopsy where lymphoma must be excluded
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging, asymmetric or B-symptom-associated lymphadenopathy suggesting lymphoma transformation
Severe autoimmune haemolysis or thrombocytopenia with bleeding
Overwhelming sepsis, particularly if the spleen has been removed
New cytopenias or organomegaly warranting re-evaluation for malignancy
reference.prognosis: Many patients have a chronic but manageable course with autoimmune cytopenias controlled by immunosuppression and lymphoproliferation that may lessen with age, but the persistently raised risk of lymphoma requires lifelong surveillance and tempers the overall outlook.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the lymphoproliferation as lymphoma and administering unnecessary chemotherapy
Performing splenectomy for cytopenias without recognising the heightened post-splenectomy sepsis risk
Overlooking the diagnosis in a child labelled as having idiopathic Evans syndrome
Failing to arrange long-term lymphoma surveillance
management: Corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin as first-line treatment of autoimmune cytopenias during acute episodes
Steroid-sparing immunosuppression with sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor) or mycophenolate mofetil for chronic or refractory cytopenias, which also lessens lymphoproliferation
Avoid splenectomy given high relapse and overwhelming sepsis risk; where performed, ensure pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis
Lifelong surveillance for Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, evaluating enlarging or asymmetrical lymphadenopathy
Monitoring of full blood count, reticulocytes and direct antiglobulin test for evolving autoimmune complications
Molecular genetic testing of FAS, FASLG and CASP10 with genetic counselling for affected families
Multidisciplinary clinical immunology and haematology care, considering haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for severe disease
